title: Free Exercise
short: Sherbert v. Verner (1963) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972) applied strict scrutiny to burdens on religion; Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held neutral, generally applicable laws need no exemption; Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. Hialeah (1993) struck down laws that targeted a faith and were not generally applicable.
trouble: Students think Smith lets government target religion. Laws that single out religious practice still get strict scrutiny (Lukumi); Smith concerns neutral, generally applicable laws.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The Free Exercise Clause protects religious belief absolutely and religious practice strongly, but not without limit. The hard question is a law that does not target religion but burdens it: must the government grant an exemption? The answer changed in 1990. This unit teaches the religion clauses as law: what the clauses say, the tests courts use and the holdings. It takes no position on any faith or on religion itself.

head: Period
Case
Rule
rows: a substantial burden on religious practice requires a compelling interest (strict scrutiny), even from a general law
a neutral, generally applicable law needs no religious exemption; rational basis
Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah (1993)
laws that target religion, or that are not generally applicable (they forbid religious conduct while allowing comparable secular conduct), get strict scrutiny

opts.facts: Alfred Smith and Galen Black worked as counselors at a private drug treatment organization in Oregon. They were fired for ingesting peyote at a ceremony of the Native American Church, and Oregon denied them unemployment benefits because the firing was for work-related misconduct. Oregon law made peyote possession a crime with no religious exception.
opts.reasoning: Justice Scalia wrote that the right of free exercise does not relieve a person of the obligation to comply with a valid and neutral law of general applicability. Requiring a compelling interest for every such law would make each person "a law unto himself." Sherbert's test was confined to unemployment cases with individual assessments; Yoder involved other rights too. Legislatures may grant exemptions.
opts.dissent: Justice O'Connor agreed with the result but not the reasoning, and would have kept strict scrutiny. Three justices dissented.

blocks.html: Smith did not leave religion unprotected. In Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah (1993) a city adopted ordinances aimed at a faith's ritual practices while exempting nearly all other killing of animals; a law that targets religion fails neutrality, and the ordinances failed strict scrutiny, 9 to 0. The ordinances were also not generally applicable: they forbade killings for religious reasons while allowing hunting, pest control and many other killings that harmed the city's stated interests just as much. Supporters of Smith say it avoids making judges weigh the importance of religious practices and leaves exemptions to democratic choice. Its critics say the clause's text and history call for exemptions. Congress responded with RFRA.

Free exercise: Employment Division v. Smith (1990) held that neutral, generally applicable laws need no exemption. But laws that target religion or are not generally applicable (Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah (1993)) get strict scrutiny. Before 1990, Sherbert and Yoder applied strict scrutiny more broadly.

blocks.title: A general law
blocks.q: A state bans all use of drones over farmland during harvest. A farmer's faith calls for a blessing ceremony using a drone. Must the state exempt him?
steps: The law is neutral (it does not target religion) and generally applicable (no exceptions for anyone).
Under Smith, no exemption is constitutionally required.
A state RFRA or a legislative exemption could still help him.

blocks.title: Exceptions for some
blocks.q: A police department forbids officers to wear beards but grants exceptions for medical reasons. It refuses an exception to an officer whose faith requires a beard. Test?
steps: The rule allows a secular exception that undercuts its purpose (a uniform appearance) as much as a religious one would.
So it is not generally applicable, as Lukumi used the term.

blocks.html: Thinking Smith lets government target religion. Laws that single out religious practice still get strict scrutiny (Lukumi); Smith concerns neutral, generally applicable laws. Check both words: neutral (no targeting) and generally applicable (no favored secular exceptions).
